title: The Place No One Could Enter… Until Love Tore the Veil
paragraphs:
The Place No One Could Enter… Until Love Tore the Veil
Understanding the Deep Meaning of the Holy of Holies—and Why Your Greatest Scandal Can Become God's Greatest Display of Grace
There are places on earth people dream of entering.
Exclusive rooms where only a privileged few are welcomed.
But for over a thousand years, there existed one place infinitely more sacred than every throne room, every temple, every kingdom, and every treasure ever built by human hands.
No king could casually walk inside.
No prophet dared enter whenever he wished.
Not even Israel's high priest approached it without trembling.
It was called the Holy of Holies.
But because God chose to dwell there.
Because the greatest story of the Holy of Holies has never been about a room.
It has always been about a relationship.
It has always been about humanity desperately longing to come home to the God we abandoned.
It has always been about Jesus.
Imagine standing outside the Tabernacle in the wilderness.
Priests move carefully through sacred rituals.
Yet everyone knows one terrifying truth.
Inside rests the Ark of the Covenant.
Above it are the golden cherubim.
Between them shines the visible manifestation of God's glorious presence—the Shekinah, from the Hebrew root שָׁכַן (šāḵan) meaning "to dwell."
God Himself had chosen to dwell among His covenant people.
"There I will meet with you, and from above the mercy seat, from between the two cherubim... I will speak with you."
Yet no ordinary Israelite could ever enter.
Because sin destroys everything it touches.
Habakkuk 1:13 says God's eyes are too pure to approve evil.
"Your iniquities have separated you from your God."
Sin is never merely breaking rules.
Humanity did not merely become imperfect.
We missed the entire purpose for which we were created.
From Eden onward, humanity has hidden behind its own fig leaves.
Once each year—and only once—the High Priest entered the Holy of Holies.
This occurred on Yom Kippur (יוֹם כִּפּוּר), the Day of Atonement, described in Leviticus 16.

The Hebrew verb כָּפַר (kāpar) means "to cover," "to make atonement," or "to reconcile." The sacrifices under the old covenant symbolically covered sin, pointing forward to the complete forgiveness God would provide through Christ. Hebrews later explains that the blood of bulls and goats could never finally remove sin; they served as shadows anticipating the perfect sacrifice (Hebrews 10:1–4).
Before entering, the High Priest bathed.
Burned incense so the cloud covered the mercy seat.
Because approaching a holy God casually meant death.
A carpenter from Nazareth walked toward Jerusalem.
The Greek New Testament calls Him:
The Hebrew equivalent is יֵשׁוּעַ (Yēšūa‘), meaning "The LORD saves."
He was not merely another priest.
He became both High Priest and Sacrifice.
"But when Christ appeared as a high priest... He entered once for all into the holy places... by means of His own blood, thus securing an eternal redemption."
Then came the moment that changed history forever.
"The debt has been paid in full."
At that exact moment Matthew records:
"And behold, the curtain of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom." (Matthew 27:51)
God tore what humanity never could.

The veil separating the Holy of Holies—traditionally understood to be massive and imposing—was removed by God's own action, signifying that through Christ's sacrificial death the barrier between God and humanity had been opened (cf. Hebrews 10:19–22).
The message could not be clearer.
Not because humanity finally became good enough.
"Therefore, brothers and sisters, since we have confidence to enter the Most Holy Place by the blood of Jesus..."
This is why the Holy of Holies matters today.
Because many people still live as though the veil remains.
They believe God merely tolerates them.
They think they must earn forgiveness.
They imagine God waiting to reject them.
The Shepherd searches for lost sheep.
Grace is not God's backup plan.
Grace is His eternal purpose accomplished in Christ.
Perhaps you carry secrets no one knows.
Maybe your greatest scandal still whispers that you are too damaged for God.
The Gospel answers with astonishing clarity.
No scandal is greater than the cross.
No sin is deeper than grace.
No darkness is stronger than Christ's light.
"Where sin increased, grace abounded all the more."
The Greek word translated "abounded all the more" is:
Grace did not merely match sin.

That does not excuse sin. Scripture never treats grace as permission to continue in rebellion (Romans 6:1–2). Rather, God's grace forgives, transforms, and calls us into a new life of holiness through Christ.
That is why our story is always...
The Holy of Holies is no longer merely a room in ancient history.

Through Christ, believers themselves are described as God's temple, indwelt by His Spirit (1 Corinthians 3:16; 6:19). The living God now dwells with His people through the Holy Spirit, anticipating the day when His redeemed people will dwell with Him forever in the new creation (Revelation 21:3).
If this truth awakened something inside you, don't let it stop here.
Someone is carrying shame they have never spoken aloud. Sometimes one shared testimony becomes the doorway through which another soul encounters the Gospel.
It may be the encouragement they have been praying for without knowing it.

And be honest before the Lord. Which part of this message spoke most deeply to your heart? Did it remind you that Christ has welcomed you into God's presence? Did it expose an area where you have been trying to earn what Jesus has already secured? Your testimony may strengthen another believer who is fighting the very same battle.
One soul reaching another has always been God's favourite way of changing the world.
